A 7-day trial with temporarily implanted percutaneous electrodes reduced her pain from 8/10 to 3/10. The implanting center has the facilities and staff for training and follow-up. The only pre-implant evaluation was a history and physical examination by the implanting neurosurgeon; the surgeon's note states that no psychological evaluation or other team evaluation was performed because she 'seems well adjusted.' Request: permanent spinal cord stimulator implantation.
cases.note: Screening done only by the implanting surgeon; no multidisciplinary team and no psychological evaluation was performed.

cases.vignette: 66-year-old man with low back pain radiating to the left leg for 4 months. He has taken over-the-counter ibuprofen only; he has not tried physical therapy, neuropathic medications, psychological therapy, or a surgical consultation, and none of these is contraindicated for him. He wants to avoid medications and asks for a spinal cord stimulator. A multidisciplinary team performed physical and psychological evaluations, and a temporary electrode trial gave 70% relief. The center has the facilities and staff for follow-up. Request: permanent spinal cord stimulator implantation.
cases.note: Stimulator proposed early: pain for 4 months, only NSAIDs tried, no contraindication to other therapies.

cases.vignette: 61-year-old woman with chronic intractable post-thoracotomy neuropathic pain for 3 years. Multiple medications, intercostal nerve blocks, physical therapy, and psychological pain management did not prove satisfactory, and surgery is judged unsuitable. A multidisciplinary team completed physical and psychological evaluations. A 7-day trial with temporarily implanted epidural electrodes produced no change in her pain (8/10 before and during the trial) or function. The center has the facilities and staff. The surgeon plans permanent implantation anyway, hoping different programming will help.
cases.note: Temporary electrode trial was done but showed no pain relief.

cases.vignette: 62-year-old man on Medicare through disability with chronic intractable central post-stroke pain of the left body for 5 years after a right thalamic stroke. Anticonvulsants, antidepressants, opioids, physical therapy, and psychological therapy did not prove satisfactory; motor cortex surgery and other surgical options were judged unsuitable by neurosurgery. A multidisciplinary pain team performed physical and psychological evaluations before implantation. A temporarily implanted stereotactic deep brain electrode, externalized for 5 days, reduced his pain from 9/10 to 4/10. The academic center has the facilities, equipment, and personnel for diagnosis, training, programming, and follow-up. Request: permanent stereotactic deep brain stimulator implantation for pain.
cases.note: Deep brain stimulation for chronic intractable pain is explicitly covered when all conditions are met.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old woman with chronic intractable neuropathic leg pain for 4 years after lumbar surgery. Medications, physical therapy, and cognitive behavioral therapy did not prove satisfactory, and further surgery is judged unsuitable. A 7-day trial with temporarily implanted percutaneous epidural electrodes reduced her pain from 7/10 to 2/10. The implanting center has the facilities, equipment, and staff for training and follow-up. The submitted records consist of the pain physician's notes, the trial report, and the operative plan; they do not mention any pre-implant screening by a multidisciplinary team or any psychological evaluation. Request: permanent spinal cord stimulator implantation.
cases.note: The record is silent on any pre-implant multidisciplinary or psychological screening.

cases.vignette: 72-year-old man with chronic intractable lower-extremity neuropathic pain for 6 years after spinal surgery. Medications, physical therapy, injections, and psychological pain management did not prove satisfactory; further surgery is judged unsuitable. A multidisciplinary team performed physical and psychological evaluations and recommended neurostimulation. The center has the necessary facilities and staff. The request for a permanent spinal cord stimulator includes the team evaluations and the operative plan; the records contain no report of a temporary electrode trial and do not say whether one was performed.
cases.note: No record of whether a temporary electrode trial occurred; contrast with the case that explicitly skipped it.

cases.vignette: 65-year-old woman with chronic intractable leg and back pain for 5 years after lumbar fusion. Medications, physical therapy, and psychological therapy did not prove satisfactory, and surgery is judged unsuitable. A multidisciplinary team at a university pain center performed physical and psychological evaluations, and a temporary electrode trial reduced her pain from 8/10 to 3/10. The permanent implant is scheduled at a small rural surgery center chosen for convenience. That center has no staff trained in stimulator programming or patient device training, no programming equipment, and no arrangement for follow-up care after implantation.
cases.note: Facility lacks follow-up and programming personnel/equipment and has no follow-up arrangement.

cases.vignette: 73-year-old woman with marked right quadriceps atrophy after 8 weeks in a long-leg cast for a tibial plateau fracture. Nerve conduction studies and EMG of the right lower limb are normal, showing intact peripheral nerve supply; she has no neurologic disease. Her physician prescribes a home NMES device to stimulate the resting quadriceps to treat the disuse atrophy.
cases.note: Disuse atrophy from casting with intact nerve supply.

cases.vignette: 66-year-old man with tibialis anterior and peroneal muscle atrophy 5 months after a traumatic laceration of the left common peroneal nerve at the fibular head. EMG shows complete denervation of the anterior and lateral compartment muscles with no voluntary motor units. His physician prescribes a home NMES device to treat the muscle atrophy.
cases.note: Atrophy from denervation (nerve supply not intact), not disuse atrophy.

cases.vignette: 70-year-old man with atrophy of the left forearm and hand muscles from disuse caused by contracture of burn scars over the left elbow and wrist, sustained 6 months ago. Nerve conduction studies show intact median, ulnar, and radial nerve function. He also has hypertension and type 2 diabetes without neuropathy. His physician prescribes an NMES device to treat the disuse atrophy.
cases.note: Disuse atrophy from burn scar contracture is one of the NCD's listed examples; nerves intact.

cases.vignette: 54-year-old man on Medicare through disability with a complete T10 spinal cord injury from a fall 2 years ago, including spinal stabilization surgery 2 years ago; neurologically stable since. Lower motor units L1 and below are intact on EMG and nerve conduction testing. He shows brisk muscle contractions to NMES with adequate sensory perception, transfers independently, stands independently in a frame for 5 minutes, has normal hand function to work the controls, has stable joints and upper and lower extremity strength to hold an upright posture, and has no hip or knee degenerative disease, osteoporotic fractures, pacemaker, severe scoliosis or osteoporosis, skin disease or cancer at the stimulation sites, irreversible contracture, or autonomic dysreflexia. He is highly motivated and committed to long-term use. Over the past 3 months he completed exactly 32 sessions of one-on-one training with the FES device, each performed directly by a physical therapist in an outpatient hospital department, aimed at walking. His physician orders an FES device for walking.
cases.note: Boundary: exactly 32 one-on-one PT sessions over 3 months; all FES characteristics met.

cases.vignette: 48-year-old woman on Medicare through disability with an incomplete T8 spinal cord injury 3 years ago; she has had no surgery for over 2 years. Lower motor units L1 and below are intact. She has brisk muscle contractions to NMES with sufficient sensory perception, transfers independently, stands independently for 4 minutes, has full hand function, stable joints, and no hip or knee degenerative disease, osteoporotic fracture, pacemaker, severe scoliosis or osteoporosis, skin lesions at stimulation sites, contracture, or autonomic dysreflexia. She is highly motivated and willing to use the device long-term. Over 3 months she completed 24 one-on-one training sessions with the FES device, each performed directly by a physical therapist at an outpatient hospital, aimed at walking. Her physician now orders an FES device for walking.
cases.note: Only 24 training sessions completed; at least 32 are required.

cases.vignette: 51-year-old man on Medicare through disability with a complete T11 spinal cord injury 4 years ago, with no surgery since the initial stabilization. Lower motor units L1 and below are intact. He has brisk muscle contractions to NMES with sufficient sensory perception, transfers independently, stands independently for 6 minutes, has full hand function, stable joints, and none of the listed contraindications (no pacemaker, severe scoliosis or osteoporosis, skin lesions, contracture, autonomic dysreflexia, hip or knee degenerative disease, or osteoporotic fracture). He is motivated and willing to use the device long-term. Over 3 months he completed 36 FES walking training sessions at an outpatient hospital; all sessions were group classes of three patients led by a physical therapist assistant. His physician orders an FES device for walking.
cases.note: Training was given by a PT assistant in a group class, not directly by the physical therapist one-on-one.

cases.vignette: 62-year-old man with an incomplete T9 spinal cord injury 3 years ago; last surgery 3 years ago. Lower motor units L1 and below are intact. He has brisk muscle contractions to NMES with adequate sensory perception, transfers independently, stands independently for 5 minutes, has full hand function to operate the controls, stable joints, no hip or knee degenerative disease, no osteoporotic fracture, no severe scoliosis or osteoporosis, no skin disease at stimulation sites, no contracture, and no autonomic dysreflexia. He has a dual-chamber cardiac pacemaker implanted 2 years ago for complete heart block. He is motivated and committed to long-term use. Over 3 months he completed 34 one-on-one FES training sessions performed directly by a physical therapist at an outpatient hospital, aimed at walking. His physician orders an FES device for walking.
cases.note: Cardiac pacemaker is an explicit FES exclusion, hidden among satisfied criteria.

cases.vignette: 46-year-old woman on Medicare through disability (ESRD) who sustained an incomplete T10 spinal cord injury in a car crash 5 months ago, with stabilization surgery 5 months ago. Lower motor units L1 and below are intact. She has brisk muscle contractions to NMES with adequate sensory perception, transfers independently, stands independently for 4 minutes, has full hand function and stable joints, and none of the listed contraindications. She is motivated and willing to use the device long-term. Starting 2 weeks after surgery she completed 40 one-on-one FES training sessions over 3 months performed directly by a physical therapist in an outpatient hospital, aimed at walking. Her physician orders an FES device for walking.
cases.note: Injury only 5 months ago; at least 6 months post recovery required.

cases.vignette: 58-year-old man on Medicare through disability with a spinal cord injury at the conus medullaris and cauda equina from an L1 burst fracture 2 years ago. EMG shows active and chronic denervation of the quadriceps, hamstrings, and gluteal muscles bilaterally. He transfers independently, stands in a frame for 3 minutes, has full hand function, and none of the listed contraindications. He is motivated. Over 3 months he completed 33 one-on-one FES training sessions performed directly by a physical therapist at an outpatient hospital, aimed at walking. His physician orders an FES device for walking.
cases.note: Conus/cauda equina injury with lower motor neuron damage: lower motor units L1 and below are not intact.

cases.vignette: 53-year-old man on Medicare through disability with a complete T10 spinal cord injury 3 years ago; no surgery since the initial stabilization. Lower motor units L1 and below are intact. He has brisk muscle contractions to NMES with adequate sensory perception, full hand function to operate controls, stable joints, and none of the listed contraindications. He is motivated and willing to use the device long-term. Over 3 months he completed 35 one-on-one FES training sessions performed directly by a physical therapist at an outpatient hospital, aimed at walking. The physical therapy evaluation and progress notes do not address his ability to transfer or how long he can stand. His physician orders an FES device for walking.
cases.note: No documentation of transfer ability or standing tolerance; nothing indicates they are lacking.

cases.vignette: 57-year-old woman on Medicare through disability with an incomplete T7 spinal cord injury 4 years ago; last surgery 4 years ago. EMG confirms intact lower motor units L1 and below. She transfers independently, stands independently for 5 minutes, has full hand function, stable joints, and none of the listed contraindications. She is motivated and willing to use the device long-term. Over 3 months she completed 32 one-on-one FES training sessions performed directly by a physical therapist at an outpatient hospital, aimed at walking. The training notes record session dates and distances but nowhere describe the muscles' contraction response to stimulation or her sensory perception of the stimulation. Her physician orders an FES device for walking.
cases.note: Muscle response to NMES and sensory perception are not documented.

cases.vignette: 52-year-old man, Medicare-eligible through disability, with focal-onset (partial onset) epilepsy, ICD-10-CM G40.219, since age 30. He has 6-10 focal impaired-awareness seizures per month despite adequate trials of four antiseizure medications (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, lacosamide, carbamazepine). Video-EEG monitoring at a comprehensive epilepsy center captured seizures arising independently from both temporal lobes; the epilepsy surgery conference documented that resective surgery is not recommended. The epileptologist requests implantation of an FDA-approved VNS device for epilepsy.
cases.note: Focal (partial onset) seizures, refractory, surgery not recommended.

cases.vignette: 67-year-old woman with drug-resistant focal-onset seizures from left mesial temporal sclerosis. She underwent a left anterior temporal lobectomy 3 years ago; seizures recurred 8 months after surgery and now occur weekly despite three antiseizure medications at maximum tolerated doses. She also has a history of major depressive disorder that has been in remission on sertraline for 5 years. Her neurologist requests VNS implantation to treat the refractory partial onset seizures; the request is not for depression.
cases.note: Partial onset seizures after failed temporal lobectomy. Controlled depression is a distractor; the device is for epilepsy, so the TRD rules do not apply.

cases.vignette: 45-year-old man on Medicare through disability with idiopathic generalized epilepsy, ICD-10-CM G40.319. EEG shows generalized 3-4 Hz spike-and-wave discharges; seizures are generalized tonic-clonic and absence, with no focal onset on video-EEG. He continues to have 4 generalized tonic-clonic seizures per month despite valproate, lamotrigine, and levetiracetam. The epilepsy center documented that surgery is not recommended because there is no focal onset. His neurologist requests VNS implantation.
cases.note: Generalized epilepsy, not partial onset; other seizure types are nationally non-covered.

cases.vignette: 58-year-old woman with medically refractory focal-onset seizures (3-5 per month after trials of four antiseizure medications). MRI shows a small left temporal cavernous malformation concordant with video-EEG onset. The epilepsy surgery conference recommends lesionectomy, which they rate as having a high chance of seizure freedom. The patient declines resective surgery because she fears brain surgery and asks for VNS instead. The neurologist submits a request for VNS implantation.
cases.note: Surgery is recommended and has not been tried or failed; patient prefers VNS.

cases.vignette: 62-year-old man with recurrent unipolar major depressive disorder confirmed by DSM-5 criteria and a structured clinical interview. The current episode has lasted 3 years. An antidepressant treatment history tool documents six failed treatments of adequate dose and duration, including ECT. MADRS scores were 34 and 36 at two visits 3 weeks apart, both within 45 days of the planned implant date. His medications have been unchanged for 10 weeks. He has no psychotic features, bipolar disorder, cognitive disorder, or suicidal intent. His psychiatrist requests VNS implantation as part of routine clinical care; he is not enrolled in any clinical study.
cases.note: TRD patient meets every patient criterion but would be implanted in routine clinical care, outside a CMS-approved CED study.

cases.vignette: 66-year-old woman with unipolar major depressive disorder confirmed by DSM-5 criteria and a structured clinical interview. Her current major depressive episode began exactly 2 years (24 months) before the planned implant. A validated antidepressant treatment history instrument documents exactly four prior failed treatments of adequate dose and duration. HAM-D-24 scores of 30 and 29 were recorded at two visits 28 days apart, both within the 45 days before the planned implant. Her medication regimen has been stable for 6 weeks. She has no current or lifetime psychotic features, psychotic disorders, bipolar disorder, cognitive disorder, current suicidal intent, or investigational treatments. She is enrolled in a CMS-approved, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled VNS trial listed on the CMS CED website, and an FDA-approved VNS device will be implanted.
cases.note: Boundaries: current episode exactly 2 years, exactly 4 failed treatments; enrolled in a CMS-approved trial.

cases.vignette: 71-year-old man with recurrent unipolar major depressive disorder (five lifetime episodes including the current one), confirmed by DSM-5 criteria and a structured clinical assessment. A treatment history tool documents five failed adequate treatments. MADRS scores of 33 and 35 were recorded at two visits 20 days apart within the 45 days before the scheduled implant. He has no psychotic features, psychotic disorder, bipolar disorder, cognitive disorder, suicidal intent, or investigational treatment. He is enrolled in a CMS-approved, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled VNS trial. Two weeks before the scheduled implant date his psychiatrist added lithium augmentation to his venlafaxine; implantation is planned on the original date.
cases.note: Lithium augmentation added 2 weeks before implant; regimen not stable for 4 weeks.

cases.vignette: 64-year-old woman with recurrent unipolar major depressive disorder confirmed by DSM-5 criteria and a structured clinical interview; current episode duration 30 months. A treatment history tool documents five failed adequate treatments. MADRS scores were 31 and 32 at two visits 25 days apart within the 45 days before implant. Medications unchanged for 8 weeks. No bipolar disorder, cognitive disorder, current suicidal intent, or investigational treatments. Her history notes that during a major depressive episode 12 years ago she had mood-congruent delusions of guilt that resolved with treatment; none since. She is enrolled in a CMS-approved, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled VNS trial.
cases.note: Lifetime history of psychotic features in a prior MDE, even though resolved, is an exclusion.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old man with unipolar major depressive disorder confirmed by DSM-5 criteria and a structured clinical interview; the current episode has lasted 4 years. MADRS scores were 35 and 34 at two visits 3 weeks apart within the 45 days before the planned implant. His current medications (bupropion and mirtazapine) have been stable for 3 months. No psychotic features, psychotic disorder, bipolar disorder, cognitive disorder, suicidal intent, or investigational treatments. He is enrolled in a CMS-approved, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled VNS trial. The record lists only his current medications; it contains no history of prior antidepressant trials, their doses or durations, and no treatment-history assessment tool.
cases.note: No record of prior treatment trials or a treatment-history tool; nothing shows the criterion is unmet.

cases.vignette: 63-year-old woman with recurrent unipolar major depressive disorder (four episodes including the current one), confirmed by DSM-5 criteria and a structured clinical interview. A treatment history tool documents six failed adequate treatments. Her medications have been stable for 7 weeks. No psychotic features, psychotic disorder, bipolar disorder, cognitive disorder, suicidal intent, or investigational treatments. She is enrolled in a CMS-approved, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled VNS trial. Psychiatry notes from two visits in the past month describe 'persistent severe depression,' but no depression rating scale scores are recorded in the chart.
cases.note: No depression scale scores recorded within the 45 days before implant; only narrative notes.

cases.vignette: 68-year-old man who received a VNS device for treatment-resistant depression 7 years ago as a participant in a CMS-approved, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled VNS trial, and who continues in that study's CMS-approved prospective longitudinal extension. Device interrogation shows the generator has reached end of battery life. His psychiatrist requests replacement of the pulse generator.
cases.note: Replacement for battery end of life in a TRD patient implanted (and still followed) within the CMS-approved study.

cases.vignette: 70-year-old man with idiopathic Parkinson's disease for 6 years, tremor-dominant form, with rest and postural tremor of the right arm plus mild rigidity of the right wrist. His tremor has responded poorly to levodopa, pramipexole and trihexyphenidyl at optimized doses, and no Hoehn and Yahr stage is recorded. Right-arm tremor is level 3 on the Fahn-Tolosa-Marin scale; he can no longer write, button shirts or use utensils with his right hand. He has a dual-chamber cardiac pacemaker for sick sinus syndrome; cardiology and the DBS team have documented a plan for device interaction precautions. MoCA 27/30, no depression, psychosis or substance use, and no major comorbidities. Requesting left thalamic VIM DBS to treat the right arm. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services. The patient is willing and able to cooperate during the awake procedure and with post-operative programming and medication adjustments.
cases.note: VIM for tremor-dominant idiopathic PD at the exact FTM boundary (level 3). Poor L-dopa response of tremor and no H&Y are irrelevant for VIM; pacemaker is a caution only.

cases.vignette: 61-year-old woman with idiopathic Parkinson's disease for 11 years (bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor). Hoehn and Yahr stage 3 off medication; UPDRS III 47 off and 19 on in a formal levodopa challenge, with clearly defined on periods. On optimized levodopa, rasagiline, a dopamine agonist and amantadine she still has disabling dyskinesias and 4 hours a day of off time. She had major depression 9 years ago, treated and in sustained remission on sertraline; the neuropsychologist documents MoCA 28/30 and concludes her mood history would neither be worsened by DBS nor interfere with benefit. Past surgery: lumbar laminectomy and a thoracic spinal cord stimulator implanted 3 years ago for radicular pain; neurosurgery has documented a plan to manage the stimulator during and after DBS. No psychosis or substance use. Requesting bilateral STN DBS. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services. The patient is willing and able to cooperate during the awake procedure and with post-operative programming and medication adjustments.
cases.note: STN DBS with distractors: remitted depression judged not to be worsened or interfere; spinal cord stimulator is an 'other electronically controlled implant' caution only; remote surgery outside the brain.

cases.vignette: 81-year-old man with essential tremor for 30 years: postural and kinetic tremor of both hands with no other neurologic signs. Left-hand tremor is level 4 on the Fahn-Tolosa-Marin scale and right-hand tremor level 3; he is left-handed and cannot drink, eat or sign his name despite maximum tolerated propranolol, primidone and topiramate. He had alcohol use disorder in his 50s and has been abstinent for 15 years. MoCA 26/30 with normal neuropsychological testing for age; no depression or psychosis. He has well-controlled hypertension and a right knee replacement; anesthesia and neurosurgery find no contraindication to surgery. Requesting right thalamic VIM DBS, with the left hand as the extremity intended for treatment. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services. The patient is willing and able to cooperate during the awake procedure and with post-operative programming and medication adjustments.
cases.note: VIM for ET with remote (not current) alcohol use disorder; treated limb FTM 4; age 81 is not a criterion.

cases.vignette: 68-year-old man with idiopathic Parkinson's disease for 10 years (rigidity, bradykinesia and intermittent rest tremor). Hoehn and Yahr stage 3; UPDRS III 41 off and 17 on with clearly defined on periods. Despite optimized levodopa, entacapone and amantadine he has disabling peak-dose dyskinesias and motor fluctuations. Three years ago he had visual hallucinations after a dopamine agonist was started; they resolved when the agonist was stopped and have not recurred. MoCA 27/30, no depression, no substance use. Brain MRI shows a small chronic right cerebellar infarct that neurology judges unrelated to his parkinsonism and neurosurgery judges no contraindication to surgery or stimulation. Prior surgery: appendectomy and cataract extraction. He has been counseled to avoid diathermy and MRI after implantation. Requesting bilateral GPi DBS. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services. The patient is willing and able to cooperate during the awake procedure and with post-operative programming and medication adjustments.
cases.note: GPi DBS; levodopa-induced hallucinations resolved 3 years ago (not current psychosis); incidental cerebellar infarct judged not a contraindication and not the etiology; post-implant MRI/diathermy avoidance is a caution.

cases.vignette: 72-year-old woman with essential tremor: postural and kinetic tremor of both hands without other neurologic signs, level 4 on the Fahn-Tolosa-Marin scale in the right hand, unable to feed herself or write despite propranolol, primidone and gabapentin. No rigidity, bradykinesia or parkinsonian features; DaT imaging is normal. MoCA 29/30, no depression, psychosis or substance use, and no significant comorbidities. Her surgeon prefers the subthalamic target, and the request is for bilateral STN DBS for her essential tremor. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services. The patient is willing and able to cooperate during the awake procedure and with post-operative programming and medication adjustments.
cases.note: Target distinction: ET meets every VIM criterion, but STN DBS is covered only for PD.

cases.vignette: 63-year-old man with idiopathic Parkinson's disease for 5 years, tremor-dominant, with rest tremor of the right arm, rigidity and bradykinesia. Hoehn and Yahr stage 3; UPDRS III 38 off. Right-arm tremor is level 4 on the Fahn-Tolosa-Marin scale and keeps him from eating or writing despite optimized medical therapy. In a formal levodopa challenge his UPDRS III improved by 6% and his tremor did not change; he and his wife describe no clearly defined on periods at any dose. MoCA 28/30, no depression, psychosis or substance use, no significant comorbidities. Requesting left GPi DBS. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services. The patient is willing and able to cooperate during the awake procedure and with post-operative programming and medication adjustments.
cases.note: Target distinction: tremor-dominant PD with FTM 4 would meet VIM criteria, but GPi is requested and GPi requires L-dopa response with clearly defined on periods.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old woman with essential tremor: postural and kinetic tremor of both hands without other neurologic signs, on maximum tolerated propranolol and primidone. Fahn-Tolosa-Marin ratings are level 4 in the right hand and level 2 in the left hand. She asks to have the left hand treated first because she works as a potter and relies on it to steady her work, though she manages all daily activities with it. MoCA 28/30, no depression, psychosis or substance use, and no significant comorbidities. Requesting unilateral right thalamic VIM DBS with the left hand as the extremity intended for treatment. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services. The patient is willing and able to cooperate during the awake procedure and with post-operative programming and medication adjustments.
cases.note: Boundary in the treated extremity: the left hand (intended for treatment) is only level 2; the level 4 right hand is not the extremity being treated.

cases.vignette: 60-year-old man referred with a header diagnosis of Parkinson's disease. He has rigidity and bradykinesia for 5 years with a good levodopa response and clearly defined on periods; Hoehn and Yahr stage 3, UPDRS III 40 off and 18 on, with disabling motor fluctuations and dyskinesias despite optimized levodopa, rasagiline and amantadine. He takes midodrine and has an indwelling urinary catheter. Last year's autonomic clinic note, after tilt-table and urodynamic testing, revised his diagnosis to probable multiple system atrophy, parkinsonian type, and the movement disorders neurologist agrees. MoCA 28/30, no depression, psychosis or substance use. Requesting bilateral STN DBS. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services. The patient is willing and able to cooperate during the awake procedure and with post-operative programming and medication adjustments.
cases.note: Parkinson-plus buried in the history: the referral header says PD, but the diagnosis was revised to MSA-P.

cases.vignette: 57-year-old man with disabling rest, postural and kinetic tremor of the right arm, level 4 on the Fahn-Tolosa-Marin scale, unable to feed himself or write despite trials of levodopa, propranolol, primidone and clonazepam. Two years ago he had a left basal ganglia hemorrhagic stroke from hypertension; his right-sided weakness recovered fully, and the tremor began 5 months after the stroke. His neurologist attributes the tremor to the stroke. He has no rigidity or bradykinesia, no family history of tremor, MoCA 27/30, no depression, psychosis or substance use, and blood pressure is now well controlled. Requesting left thalamic VIM DBS to treat the right arm. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services. The patient is willing and able to cooperate during the awake procedure and with post-operative programming and medication adjustments.
cases.note: Structural lesion as etiology: right-hand tremor followed a left basal ganglia hemorrhage and is attributed to it; not ET or PD.

cases.vignette: 66-year-old woman with idiopathic Parkinson's disease for 14 years (rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia). Hoehn and Yahr stage 3; UPDRS III 45 off and 20 on during a levodopa challenge, with clearly defined on periods. She has disabling dyskinesias and off periods despite optimized levodopa, opicapone, a dopamine agonist and amantadine. MoCA 27/30, no depression, psychosis or substance use. Surgical history: cholecystectomy (2004), left stereotactic radiofrequency pallidotomy (2017), bilateral cataract extraction (2021). Medical history: osteoporosis and hypothyroidism, both treated. Requesting bilateral GPi DBS. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services. The patient is willing and able to cooperate during the awake procedure and with post-operative programming and medication adjustments.
cases.note: Prior left pallidotomy appears only in the surgical history list; bilateral GPi DBS includes the previously operated left GPi.

cases.vignette: 74-year-old woman with essential tremor: postural and kinetic tremor of both hands without other neurologic signs. The referral letter describes the right-hand tremor as severe and says she has trouble writing and eating despite propranolol and primidone at maximum tolerated doses. No Fahn-Tolosa-Marin or other tremor rating scale score is recorded anywhere in the record. MoCA 28/30, no depression, psychosis or substance use, no significant comorbidities. Requesting left thalamic VIM DBS to treat the right hand. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services. The patient is willing and able to cooperate during the awake procedure and with post-operative programming and medication adjustments.
cases.note: No tremor rating scale score in the record; severity is only described in words, so the level 3-4 requirement is undocumented.

cases.vignette: 64-year-old man with idiopathic Parkinson's disease for 9 years (rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia). Clinic notes describe a robust levodopa response with clearly defined on periods and disabling motor fluctuations and dyskinesias despite optimized levodopa, safinamide, a dopamine agonist and amantadine. The notes are narrative; no Hoehn and Yahr stage or UPDRS score has been recorded. MoCA 28/30, no depression, psychosis or substance use, no significant comorbidities. Requesting bilateral STN DBS. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services. The patient is willing and able to cooperate during the awake procedure and with post-operative programming and medication adjustments.
cases.note: STN request with no Hoehn and Yahr stage or UPDRS III score, so advanced PD is not documented by the required scales.

cases.vignette: 67-year-old woman with idiopathic Parkinson's disease, tremor-dominant form, with rest tremor and rigidity of the left arm. Left-arm tremor is level 4 on the Fahn-Tolosa-Marin scale and keeps her from dressing and eating with that hand despite optimized levodopa, a dopamine agonist and propranolol. MoCA 29/30, no depression, psychosis or substance use, no significant comorbidities. She has an implanted cardiac loop recorder; cardiology has documented precautions. Requesting right thalamic VIM DBS to treat the left arm. The device is FDA-approved for DBS. A movement disorders neurologist selected the patient and will manage post-procedure care. The neurosurgeon is trained in the procedure and experienced in movement disorder surgery, including DBS, and in stereotactic neurosurgery; the operative team has DBS training, and the hospital has MRI/CT for stereotactic targeting, a stereotactic operating room, and the needed support services.
cases.note: Every criterion is documented except the patient's willingness and ability to cooperate during the conscious procedure and post-surgical adjustments; the record is simply silent.

cases.vignette: 70-year-old man admitted with bilateral pneumonia; bronchoscopy confirms Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. He takes no immunosuppressive drugs, has no cancer or transplant history, and no other explanation for immune compromise has been found. He has never been tested for HIV. The inpatient team orders an HIV-1/HIV-2 combination antibody enzyme immunoassay.
cases.note: Documented, otherwise unexplained Pneumocystis pneumonia (AIDS-defining opportunistic infection) supports initial HIV-1/2 antibody EIA.

cases.vignette: 67-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis C infection documented last year, seen by her hepatologist, who ordered HIV testing. The laboratory report in the chart shows that the HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay was reactive, and that repeat testing of the same serum sample in duplicate was reactive both times. A confirmatory Western blot on that sample is now requested.
cases.note: Western blot after documented repeatedly positive EIA on a single sample, in a patient with an indication (chronic hepatitis C).

cases.vignette: 72-year-old man with newly diagnosed chronic hepatitis B infection; his gastroenterologist orders HIV testing. The laboratory report shows that the initial HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay was reactive once. The laboratory notes that the sample was not re-tested by EIA, and no second EIA was run on it. The physician orders a Western blot on the same sample.
cases.note: Western blot ordered after a single reactive EIA that was never repeated; the NCD requires documented repeatedly positive or equivocal EIA first.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old woman with recurrent oral and esophageal candidiasis with no other explanation, seen by an infectious disease physician. The referral letter states that she 'had a positive HIV screen elsewhere' and asks for confirmation. The infectious disease physician orders a Western blot. The chart contains no laboratory report of the prior enzyme immunoassay, and no information on whether it was repeated or on what sample.
cases.note: Western blot requested, but there is no EIA result in the record to show it was repeatedly positive or equivocal; nothing shows it was not.

cases.vignette: 66-year-old man who moved to a new city and is establishing care with a new primary care physician. Two years ago his HIV infection was diagnosed by a repeatedly reactive HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay and a positive Western blot, and the reports are in his transferred records. He takes antiretroviral therapy. The new physician orders a repeat HIV antibody enzyme immunoassay and Western blot 'to re-establish the diagnosis in our system.'
cases.note: HIV infection was confirmed by EIA and Western blot 2 years ago; repeat diagnostic testing is not indicated.

cases.vignette: 68-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis C infection; her HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay 6 weeks ago was negative. Since then she has had no new exposures, she has no fever, rash, lymphadenopathy or other symptoms, and her physician documents that there is no indication for viral RNA testing. At today's follow-up the physician orders a repeat HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay 'to be sure.'
cases.note: Negative EIA 6 weeks ago with no indication for RNA testing; retesting should wait 3-6 months.

cases.vignette: 71-year-old man with otherwise unexplained weight loss of 9 kg over 6 months, chronic diarrhea and generalized lymphadenopathy. His internist orders an HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay, and separately orders a standalone HIV-1 p24 antigen assay to diagnose HIV infection. The request under review is the standalone p24 antigen assay.
cases.note: Standalone p24 antigen assay ordered to diagnose HIV; the NCD states HIV antigen tests have no defined diagnostic usage.

cases.vignette: 66-year-old man presents with 10 days of fever, malaise, generalized lymphadenopathy and a diffuse maculopapular skin rash, beginning 3 weeks after unprotected anal intercourse with a new partner. His HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay drawn at this visit is negative. The infectious disease physician documents that serology has not established a diagnosis but strong clinical suspicion of acute HIV infection persists, and orders HIV-1 viral RNA detection.
cases.note: Exception to serology-first: signs of acute retroviral syndrome with a negative EIA; strong suspicion persists, so viral RNA detection is appropriate.

cases.vignette: 65-year-old nurse who sustained a deep needle-stick injury with a hollow-bore needle used on a patient in the emergency department, documented in an occupational health incident report. The source patient's HIV status is unknown and the source left before testing. Post-exposure antiviral prophylaxis was started within 2 hours. The occupational health physician orders a baseline HIV-1/2 antibody enzyme immunoassay.
cases.note: Documented needle-stick exposure with post-exposure antiviral therapy initiated. Unknown source status is a distractor.

cases.vignette: 74-year-old woman with 2 years of progressive memory loss. Neuropsychological testing shows amnestic mild cognitive impairment (MMSE 26, CDR 0.5) and her neurologist diagnoses MCI due to Alzheimer's disease. Amyloid PET is positive. Requesting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody that received FDA traditional approval for Alzheimer's disease based on a direct measure of clinical benefit. Treatment will be given according to the FDA-approved label by a multidisciplinary dementia team, and the patient is enrolled in a CMS-approved prospective comparative study that collects data in a registry.
cases.note: MCI due to AD, amyloid PET positive, traditional-approval drug in a CMS-approved registry study.

cases.vignette: 71-year-old man with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (MMSE 25, CDR 0.5) clinically attributed to Alzheimer's disease. Amyloid PET was read as negative for amyloid plaques. Requesting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody that received FDA traditional approval for Alzheimer's disease based on a direct measure of clinical benefit. Treatment will be given according to the FDA-approved label by a multidisciplinary dementia team, and the patient is enrolled in a CMS-approved prospective comparative study that collects data in a registry.
cases.note: Amyloid PET negative.

cases.vignette: 76-year-old woman with mild Alzheimer's disease dementia (MMSE 22, CDR 1). The referral letter says amyloid testing was done at another hospital, but no PET report, CSF result or other amyloid result is in the record. Requesting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody that received FDA traditional approval for Alzheimer's disease based on a direct measure of clinical benefit. Treatment will be given according to the FDA-approved label by a multidisciplinary dementia team, and the patient is enrolled in a CMS-approved prospective comparative study that collects data in a registry.
cases.note: Amyloid test reportedly done elsewhere; no result in the record.

cases.vignette: 79-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease dementia of moderate severity (MMSE 14, CDR 2), needing help with dressing and bathing. Amyloid PET is positive. Requesting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody that received FDA traditional approval for Alzheimer's disease based on a direct measure of clinical benefit. Treatment will be given according to the FDA-approved label by a multidisciplinary dementia team, and the patient is enrolled in a CMS-approved prospective comparative study that collects data in a registry.
cases.note: Moderate dementia exceeds MCI/mild dementia.

cases.vignette: 73-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease (MMSE 27, CDR 0.5), amyloid confirmed by CSF biomarkers. Requesting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody that received FDA traditional approval for Alzheimer's disease based on a direct measure of clinical benefit, to be given at a community infusion center per the FDA label. She is not enrolled in any CMS-approved study, registry, or NIH-supported trial.
cases.note: Traditional-approval drug but not in any CMS-approved study or registry.

cases.vignette: 70-year-old man with mild Alzheimer's disease dementia (MMSE 23, CDR 1), amyloid PET positive. Requesting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody that received FDA accelerated approval for Alzheimer's disease based on amyloid reduction (a surrogate endpoint), without a direct measure of clinical benefit. Treatment will be given according to the FDA-approved label by a multidisciplinary dementia team, and the patient is enrolled in a CMS-approved prospective comparative study that collects data in a registry.
cases.note: Accelerated-approval drug requires an RCT under IND; a registry study is not enough.

cases.vignette: 72-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease (MMSE 26, CDR 0.5), amyloid PET positive. Requesting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody that received FDA accelerated approval for Alzheimer's disease based on amyloid reduction (a surrogate endpoint), without a direct measure of clinical benefit. She is enrolled in a randomized controlled trial of this drug conducted under an investigational new drug (IND) application.
cases.note: Accelerated-approval drug given within an RCT under an IND.

cases.vignette: 68-year-old man with mild Alzheimer's disease dementia (MMSE 24, CDR 1), amyloid PET positive. Requesting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody that received FDA traditional approval for Alzheimer's disease based on a direct measure of clinical benefit. He is enrolled in an NIH-supported trial, and the drug is given according to its FDA-approved indication.
cases.note: NIH-supported trial per FDA indication.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old woman with subjective memory complaints. Comprehensive neuropsychological testing is within normal limits for age and education (MMSE 29, CDR 0) and she is fully independent. An amyloid PET done in a screening program was positive. Requesting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody that received FDA traditional approval for Alzheimer's disease based on a direct measure of clinical benefit. Treatment will be given according to the FDA-approved label by a multidisciplinary dementia team, and the patient is enrolled in a CMS-approved prospective comparative study that collects data in a registry.
cases.note: Subjective cognitive decline with normal testing is not MCI.

cases.vignette: 75-year-old man with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease (MMSE 25, CDR 0.5). CSF testing shows a low amyloid-beta 42/40 ratio and elevated p-tau consistent with Alzheimer's pathology. Requesting an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody that received FDA traditional approval for Alzheimer's disease based on a direct measure of clinical benefit. Treatment will be given according to the FDA-approved label by a multidisciplinary dementia team, and the patient is enrolled in a CMS-approved prospective comparative study that collects data in a registry.
cases.note: Amyloid confirmed by CSF rather than PET is acceptable.

cases.vignette: 71-year-old postmenopausal woman seen by her nurse practitioner for a preventive visit. Her last Pap smear, 36 months ago, was negative, as were all prior Pap smears. She has had two lifetime sexual partners, began sexual activity at age 20, has no history of sexually transmitted disease, and no DES exposure. The nurse practitioner orders and collects a screening Pap smear.
cases.note: Low-risk postmenopausal woman whose last Pap smear was 36 months ago: no such test in the preceding two years.

cases.vignette: 68-year-old postmenopausal woman seen by her family physician for her annual visit. She had a negative Pap smear 13 months ago and four negative Pap smears in the previous seven years, with no abnormal results ever. She has had one lifetime sexual partner, began sexual activity at age 22, has no history of sexually transmitted disease, and no DES exposure. The physician documents her as low risk and orders a repeat screening Pap smear as part of a routine annual exam.
cases.note: Last Pap 13 months ago; she is low risk, postmenopausal (not of childbearing age), and no high-risk recommendation exists.

cases.vignette: 66-year-old postmenopausal woman seen by her internist. She had a negative Pap smear 12 months ago. Her documented history includes six lifetime sexual partners. She began sexual activity at age 18, has no history of sexually transmitted disease, and no DES exposure. Based on her history, the internist documents that she is at high risk for cervical cancer, recommends Pap smears more frequently than every two years, and orders a screening Pap smear today.
cases.note: Six lifetime partners (five or more) is a listed high-risk factor, and the physician recommends annual testing, so a Pap 12 months after the last is covered.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old postmenopausal woman seen by her family physician. She had a negative Pap smear 14 months ago and four negative Pap smears in the previous seven years, with no abnormal results ever. She has had four lifetime sexual partners, began sexual activity at age 19, has no history of sexually transmitted disease, and no DES exposure. The physician recommends annual Pap smears 'to be safe' and orders a screening Pap smear today.
cases.note: Near miss: four lifetime partners is below the five-or-more threshold and no other risk factor applies, so the physician's recommendation of annual testing does not meet the high-risk condition; last Pap 14 months ago.

cases.vignette: 73-year-old postmenopausal woman seen by her nurse practitioner. She had a negative Pap smear 12 months ago and four negative Pap smears in the previous seven years, with no abnormal results ever. She began sexual activity at age 17, has had two lifetime sexual partners, has no history of sexually transmitted disease, and no DES exposure. Citing her early start of sexual activity, the nurse practitioner documents her as high risk, recommends annual testing, and orders a screening Pap smear.
cases.note: Near miss: onset of sexual activity at 17 is not under 16; no other risk factor applies; last Pap 12 months ago.

cases.vignette: 42-year-old premenopausal woman entitled to Medicare through disability, seen by her gynecologist, who documents from her history that she is of childbearing age. A Pap smear 2 years ago showed a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion; her most recent Pap smear, 11 months ago, was negative. The gynecologist orders and collects a screening Pap smear today.
cases.note: Premenopausal woman of childbearing age (as determined by her physician) with an abnormal Pap 2 years ago, i.e., within the preceding 3 years; covered despite a Pap 11 months ago.

cases.vignette: 75-year-old postmenopausal woman seen by her family physician for a screening Pap smear and pelvic examination. Her last Pap smear and pelvic examination were 30 months ago and were normal. She is low risk, with one lifetime sexual partner and no history of sexually transmitted disease. The physician orders and performs both. The documented examination includes: inspection and palpation of both breasts; external genitalia; urethral meatus; vagina; cervix; uterus; and adnexa/parametria. A digital rectal examination, examination of the urethra, bladder, and anus and perineum were not performed.
cases.note: Screening pelvic exam with clinical breast exam including exactly seven of the eleven elements; last pelvic exam and Pap 30 months ago.

cases.vignette: 70-year-old postmenopausal woman, new to the practice, seen by a nurse practitioner. She cannot recall when she last had a Pap smear and thinks it may have been 'a year or two ago' at a clinic that has since closed; no prior cervical cytology records are available. She has had one lifetime sexual partner, began sexual activity at age 21, has no history of sexually transmitted disease, and no DES exposure. The nurse practitioner orders and collects a screening Pap smear.
cases.note: Low-risk postmenopausal woman; the date of her last Pap smear is unknown, so it cannot be confirmed that none occurred in the preceding two years.

cases.vignette: 67-year-old postmenopausal woman seen by her internist. She had a negative Pap smear 12 months ago. The note reads 'High risk - annual Pap recommended' and the internist orders a screening Pap smear. The record contains no sexual history, no history of sexually transmitted disease, no prior Pap smear history beyond last year's result, and no information on DES exposure, and gives no reason for the high-risk label.
cases.note: The physician labels her high risk and recommends annual testing, but the record contains no history or findings supporting high risk; last Pap 12 months ago.

cases.vignette: 88-year-old woman seen for a routine primary care visit on March 3, 2026. She has hypertension and osteoarthritis and no gastrointestinal symptoms. Her brother was diagnosed with colon cancer at age 70. Her last screening immunochemical FOBT, covered by Medicare, was performed on March 24, 2025 and was negative. Her nurse practitioner, who manages her care and will act on the result, signs a written order for a screening iFOBT kit, to be completed according to the manufacturer's instructions.
cases.note: Boundary: last covered FOBT in March 2025, request in March 2026, so 11 full months (April-February) have passed even though fewer than 12 calendar months by date. Age 88 and family history of colon cancer are distractors: FOBT has no upper age limit or average-risk requirement.

cases.vignette: 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia, seen for a primary care visit on February 26, 2026. He has no gastrointestinal symptoms, no personal history of polyps or colorectal cancer, and no relevant family history. His last screening guaiac FOBT, covered by Medicare, was performed on March 2, 2025 and was negative. His attending internist, who manages his care, writes a written order for a screening immunochemical FOBT to be collected per the manufacturer's instructions and processed by the hospital laboratory.
cases.note: Last covered FOBT in March 2025; request in February 2026 leaves only 10 full months (April-January) after the month of the last test.

cases.vignette: 45-year-old man (Medicare through disability) who turned 45 last month, seen by his primary care physician. He has no abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, change in bowel habits or other signs of colorectal disease, and no prior colorectal cancer screening of any kind. He has no personal history of adenomatous polyps, colorectal cancer, Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis, and no family history of colorectal cancer, adenomatous polyps, familial adenomatous polyposis or hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer. The physician, who will use the result to manage his care, orders a blood-based non-invasive biomarker screening test and documents that she gave him information about the test's performance and the importance of a follow-on colonoscopy if the result is positive. The test is FDA market authorized and indicated for colorectal cancer screening, has an FDA label reporting 83% sensitivity and 90% specificity for colorectal cancer versus colonoscopy, and is processed in a CLIA-certified laboratory.
cases.note: Boundary: age exactly 45; test meets Criteria 2 exactly (sensitivity 83% >= 79%, specificity exactly 90%) even though it fails Criteria 1.

cases.vignette: 67-year-old woman seen by her family physician for an annual visit. She is asymptomatic, with no abdominal pain, blood in stool or prior positive screening test. She has no personal history of adenomatous polyps, colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease, and no family history of colorectal cancer, adenomatous polyps, familial adenomatous polyposis or hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer. She has never had a non-invasive biomarker screening test. The physician, who will use the result in her management, orders a non-invasive biomarker colorectal cancer screening test and documents counseling about the test's performance and the need for a follow-on colonoscopy if positive. The test is FDA market authorized and indicated for colorectal cancer screening and is processed in a CLIA-certified laboratory; its FDA labeling reports a sensitivity of 88% and a specificity of 89% for colorectal cancer compared with colonoscopy.
cases.note: Sensitivity 88% / specificity 89% fails both performance options (Criteria 1 needs sensitivity >= 90%; Criteria 2 needs specificity >= 90%).

cases.vignette: 86-year-old man in good health, seen by his primary care nurse practitioner. He has no gastrointestinal symptoms, no personal history of adenomatous polyps, colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease, and no family history of colorectal cancer or polyposis syndromes. He has never had a non-invasive biomarker screening test. The nurse practitioner, who will use the result in his management, orders a blood-based non-invasive biomarker colorectal cancer screening test and documents that she explained the test's performance and the importance of a follow-on colonoscopy if positive. The test is FDA market authorized and indicated for colorectal cancer screening, has FDA-labeled sensitivity of 91% and specificity of 88% versus colonoscopy, and is processed in a CLIA-certified laboratory.
cases.note: Age 86 exceeds the 45-85 range for biomarker tests; all other biomarker criteria are met.

cases.vignette: 58-year-old woman seen by her family physician. At this visit she reports noticing blood in her stool on several occasions over the past three weeks; she is otherwise well. She has no personal history of adenomatous polyps, colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease, and no family history of colorectal cancer or polyposis syndromes. She has never had colorectal cancer screening. The physician, who will use the result in her management, orders a blood-based non-invasive biomarker colorectal cancer screening test and documents counseling about the test's performance and the need for a follow-on colonoscopy if positive. The test is FDA market authorized and indicated for colorectal cancer screening, has FDA-labeled sensitivity of 90% and specificity of 88% versus colonoscopy, and is processed in a CLIA-certified laboratory.
cases.note: Reported blood in stool is a sign of colorectal disease, so the patient is not asymptomatic as the biomarker criteria require.

cases.vignette: 71-year-old man seen by his internist for a wellness visit. He is asymptomatic, with no abdominal pain or blood in stool. A colonoscopy 6 years ago found two tubular adenomas, which were removed; he has no family history of colorectal cancer. He has never had a non-invasive biomarker screening test. The internist, who will use the result in his management, orders a blood-based non-invasive biomarker colorectal cancer screening test and documents counseling about the test's performance and the importance of a follow-on colonoscopy if positive. The test is FDA market authorized and indicated for colorectal cancer screening, has FDA-labeled sensitivity of 92% and specificity of 90% versus colonoscopy, and is processed in a CLIA-certified laboratory.
cases.note: Personal history of adenomatous polyps removed 6 years ago means the patient is not at average risk.

cases.vignette: 63-year-old woman seen by her primary care physician assistant. She is asymptomatic, with no abdominal pain, blood in stool or prior positive screening test. She has no personal history of adenomatous polyps, colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease, and no family history of colorectal cancer, adenomatous polyps, familial adenomatous polyposis or hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer. She has never had a non-invasive biomarker screening test. The physician assistant, who will use the result in her management, orders a blood-based non-invasive biomarker colorectal cancer screening test. The visit note records the order and the risk assessment but contains no documentation of any discussion of the test's performance or of follow-on colonoscopy if the result is positive. The test is FDA market authorized and indicated for colorectal cancer screening, has FDA-labeled sensitivity of 90% and specificity of 90% versus colonoscopy, and is processed in a CLIA-certified laboratory.
cases.note: All other biomarker criteria are met, but the record contains no documentation that the patient was given information about test performance and follow-on colonoscopy.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old man, new to the practice, seen by a family physician. He is asymptomatic, with no abdominal pain or blood in stool. He reports no personal history of colorectal cancer, polyps or inflammatory bowel disease. The family history section of the note reads 'not obtained - patient adopted, no information available.' He has never had a non-invasive biomarker screening test. The physician, who will use the result in his management, orders a blood-based non-invasive biomarker colorectal cancer screening test and documents counseling about the test's performance and the importance of a follow-on colonoscopy if positive. The test is FDA market authorized and indicated for colorectal cancer screening, has FDA-labeled sensitivity of 91% and specificity of 89% versus colonoscopy, and is processed in a CLIA-certified laboratory.
cases.note: Family history was not obtained, so average-risk status cannot be confirmed; nothing in the record shows elevated risk.

cases.vignette: 85-year-old woman who turned 85 two months ago, seen by her geriatrician.She has well-controlled hypothyroidism and no gastrointestinal symptoms. A colonoscopy 9 years ago was normal. She had a negative blood-based non-invasive biomarker screening test 38 months ago. She has no personal history of adenomatous polyps, colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease, and no family history of colorectal cancer, adenomatous polyps, familial adenomatous polyposis or hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer. The geriatrician, who will use the result in her management, orders a repeat non-invasive biomarker screening test and documents that she reviewed the test's performance and the importance of a follow-on colonoscopy if positive. The test is FDA market authorized and indicated for colorectal cancer screening, has FDA-labeled sensitivity of 90% and specificity of 87% versus colonoscopy, and is processed in a CLIA-certified laboratory.
cases.note: Boundary: age exactly 85; Criteria 1 met at the threshold (sensitivity 90%, specificity 87%); prior biomarker test 38 months ago (more than 3 years). A normal colonoscopy 9 years ago and well-controlled hypothyroidism are distractors.

cases.vignette: 58-year-old woman (Medicare through disability) with no reported HIV risk factors, seen by her primary care physician on February 9, 2026. Her last HIV screening test, negative, was performed on February 24, 2025. She agrees to voluntary screening, and the physician orders an FDA-approved HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody laboratory test, run in a CLIA-certified Medicare-enrolled laboratory. She has no known HIV-related illness and is not pregnant.
cases.note: Boundary: prior screen February 2025, current February 2026, so 11 full months (March-January) have elapsed. Age 58 needs no risk factors.

cases.vignette: 47-year-old man with hypertension, seen by his internist on February 20, 2026 for a routine visit. His last HIV screening test, negative, was performed on March 3, 2025. He has no known HIV-related illness. He agrees to voluntary screening, and the internist orders an FDA-approved HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody test performed by the clinic's CLIA-certified, Medicare-enrolled laboratory.
cases.note: Prior screen March 2025, current February 2026: only 10 full months (April-January) have elapsed after the month of the prior test.

cases.vignette: 72-year-old widower seen by his family physician for his annual wellness visit. During the history, he reports that he began a sexual relationship with a new partner 3 months ago. The physician documents that he is at increased risk for HIV infection because of a new sexual partner, and the patient agrees to voluntary screening. He has never had an HIV test and has no known HIV-related illness. An FDA-approved HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody test is ordered and performed by a CLIA-certified, Medicare-enrolled laboratory.
cases.note: Age over 65 with a listed increased-risk factor (new sexual partner) identified by the practitioner from the history; never screened.

cases.vignette: 74-year-old man seen by his internist for an annual wellness visit. The documented history shows a 45-year monogamous marriage, no injection drug use, no transfusions, no sexually transmitted infections, and no other HIV risk factors; the internist documents 'no HIV risk factors identified.' The patient did not ask for HIV testing. The internist adds an FDA-approved HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody screening test to his routine laboratory panel, to be run by a CLIA-certified, Medicare-enrolled laboratory. He has never had an HIV test.
cases.note: Age 74 with documented absence of all risk factors; the patient did not request the test, so he is not in the increased-risk group required over age 65.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old woman seen by her nurse practitioner for an annual wellness visit. She reports no individual HIV risk factors: no new or multiple partners, no injection drug use, no transfusions, and no sexually transmitted infections. She nonetheless asks to be tested for HIV, and the nurse practitioner documents her request and orders voluntary screening with an FDA-approved HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody test, performed by a CLIA-certified, Medicare-enrolled laboratory. She has never had an HIV test and has no known HIV-related illness.
cases.note: Exception: over 65 with no risk factors, but persons who request an HIV test despite reporting no individual risk factors are defined as increased risk.

cases.vignette: 52-year-old man with HIV infection diagnosed 6 years ago, on antiretroviral therapy with an undetectable viral load, seen by his primary care physician. His last HIV screening-type test was more than 6 years ago. The physician orders an FDA-approved HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody screening test as part of his annual preventive labs, to be run by a CLIA-certified, Medicare-enrolled laboratory.
cases.note: Known HIV infection on antiretroviral therapy; beneficiaries with a known HIV-related diagnosis are not eligible for screening.

cases.vignette: 31-year-old pregnant woman (Medicare through disability) admitted in labor at 39 weeks. She had HIV screening when her pregnancy was diagnosed at 7 weeks and again at 30 weeks (third trimester); both were negative. Her obstetrician orders voluntary HIV screening at labor with an FDA-approved point-of-care test, performed under CLIA by the hospital, an eligible Medicare provider. She has no known HIV-related illness.
cases.note: Pregnancy: third of the three specified screenings (at diagnosis, third trimester, now at labor), ordered by her clinician; the annual limit does not apply.

cases.vignette: 28-year-old pregnant woman (Medicare through disability), now at 35 weeks and not in labor. She had HIV screening when her pregnancy was diagnosed at 8 weeks and again at 29 weeks (third trimester); both were negative, and she reports no new exposures. At today's routine prenatal visit her obstetrician orders another voluntary HIV screening test with an FDA-approved laboratory test, run by a CLIA-certified, Medicare-enrolled laboratory. She has no known HIV-related illness.
cases.note: She already had screenings at diagnosis of pregnancy and in the third trimester; a second third-trimester test before labor is not one of the three specified screenings.

cases.vignette: 68-year-old woman seen by her family physician. The visit note lists her medications and blood pressure and contains an order for an FDA-approved HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody screening test, to be run by a CLIA-certified, Medicare-enrolled laboratory. The note contains no sexual history, no drug-use history, no transfusion history, no risk assessment of any kind, and no indication of whether the patient requested the test. She has never had an HIV test and has no known HIV-related illness.
cases.note: Age 68 requires increased risk, but the record contains no risk assessment and no patient request; nothing shows she lacks risk factors.

cases.vignette: 40-year-old woman (Medicare through disability) seen by her new primary care physician. She says she 'had an HIV test at another clinic sometime last year' but cannot recall the month, and records from that clinic have been requested but not received. She agrees to voluntary screening, and the physician orders an FDA-approved HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody test, to be run by a CLIA-certified, Medicare-enrolled laboratory. She has no known HIV-related illness and is not pregnant.
cases.note: Age 40 qualifies without risk factors, but she may have had a screening within the past year; the date of the prior test is unknown.

cases.vignette: 64-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. Three weeks ago at her family medicine practice her BMI was measured as 30.0 kg/m2 (weight 86.7 kg, height 1.70 m), and she began intensive behavioral therapy for obesity with a dietary assessment. Today is her third weekly face-to-face visit in the first month, with the practice's nurse practitioner, who assesses her eating and activity, gives personalized advice, agrees on goals, teaches self-monitoring techniques, and schedules the next visit. She is alert and fully competent.
cases.note: Boundary: BMI exactly 30.0. Third weekly visit in month 1, by an NP in a family medicine practice. Type 2 diabetes on metformin is a distractor.

cases.vignette: 70-year-old man with hypertension and prediabetes, seen by his general internist at his primary care practice. His BMI is calculated at 29.6 kg/m2 (weight 90.6 kg, height 1.75 m). The internist begins intensive behavioral therapy, completing a dietary assessment and a counseling session following the 5-A framework, and plans weekly visits for the first month. He is alert and fully competent.
cases.note: BMI 29.6 is below the obesity threshold of 30, despite comorbid hypertension and prediabetes.

cases.vignette: 67-year-old woman with a starting BMI of 34 kg/m2 who began intensive behavioral therapy for obesity 7 months ago with her general internist at her primary care practice. She attended weekly visits in month 1 and every-other-week visits in months 2-6. At the six-month visit the internist reassessed her obesity and documented in the office record a weight of 88.0 kg compared with 91.0 kg at the start, a loss of 3.0 kg. Today, in month 8, she attends a monthly face-to-face counseling visit with the internist. She is alert and fully competent.
cases.note: Boundary: month-8 monthly visit with exactly 3.0 kg weight loss over the first six months, documented at the six-month reassessment.

cases.vignette: 72-year-old man with a starting BMI of 36 kg/m2 who began intensive behavioral therapy for obesity 8 months ago with his family physician at his primary care practice. He attended all weekly visits in month 1 and every-other-week visits in months 2-6. At the six-month visit the physician reassessed his obesity and documented a weight of 104.5 kg compared with 107.0 kg at the start, a loss of 2.5 kg. Today, in month 9, he attends a monthly face-to-face counseling visit. He is alert and fully competent and reports improved energy.
cases.note: Only 2.5 kg lost over the first six months, so the month 7-12 monthly visits are not covered.

cases.vignette: 66-year-old woman with a starting BMI of 33 kg/m2 who began intensive behavioral therapy for obesity 6 months and 2 weeks ago with a physician assistant at her family medicine practice. She attended weekly visits in month 1 and every-other-week visits in months 2-6. The six-month visit note documents a counseling discussion but records no weight, no BMI and no determination of weight change since the start of therapy. She says she 'feels lighter.' Today, in month 7, she attends a monthly face-to-face counseling visit. She is alert and fully competent.
cases.note: Month-7 visit, but the six-month office record contains no weight or weight-loss determination; nothing shows she failed to lose 3 kg.

cases.vignette: 78-year-old woman with a BMI of 38 kg/m2, currently in a skilled nursing facility for rehabilitation after a hip fracture. Her attending physician, a geriatrician, visits her at the skilled nursing facility, performs a dietary assessment, and begins weekly face-to-face intensive behavioral counseling sessions for obesity there using the 5-A framework. She is alert and fully competent. The request is for the first weekly visit.
cases.note: Counseling delivered in a skilled nursing facility, which the NCD lists as not a primary care setting.

cases.vignette: 81-year-old woman with a BMI of 35 kg/m2 and moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's dementia, seen at her family medicine practice by her family physician. During today's visit she is disoriented to time and place and cannot follow the conversation. The physician measures her BMI, completes a dietary assessment with her daughter, and provides intensive behavioral counseling on diet and exercise to the daughter. The request is for the first weekly intensive behavioral therapy visit.
cases.note: Patient is not competent and alert at the time of counseling; counseling is directed at the daughter.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old man with a starting BMI of 37 kg/m2 who began intensive behavioral therapy for obesity 10 weeks ago with his family physician at his primary care practice; he is now in month 3. He attended weekly visits in month 1 and has been seen every other week since. His most recent face-to-face counseling visit was 7 days ago. He returns today for another face-to-face counseling visit because he wants extra support with meal planning. He is alert and fully competent.
cases.note: Month 3 allows one visit every other week; this visit is only 7 days after the previous one.

cases.vignette: 61-year-old woman (Medicare through disability) with a starting BMI of 41 kg/m2 who began intensive behavioral therapy for obesity 3 months and 2 weeks ago with a physician assistant at her family medicine practice. She attended weekly visits in month 1 and every-other-week visits since; her last face-to-face visit was 14 days ago. She also takes a GLP-1 receptor agonist prescribed by her physician and has a consultation with a bariatric surgeon scheduled next month. Today the physician assistant reviews her food log, adjusts her exercise plan, and schedules the next visit in two weeks. She is alert and fully competent.
cases.note: Month-4 every-other-week visit 14 days after the last, by a PA in a family practice. Concurrent GLP-1 medication and a pending bariatric surgery consult are distractors; the NCD does not restrict them.

cases.vignette: 73-year-old man seen by his general internist at his primary care practice to begin intensive behavioral therapy for obesity. The note records his weight as 102 kg; his height is not recorded, and no BMI appears in the note or anywhere in his chart. The internist completes a dietary assessment and a counseling session using the 5-A framework and schedules weekly follow-up for the first month. He is alert and fully competent.
cases.note: Weight is recorded but height and BMI are not, so obesity (BMI >= 30) cannot be confirmed; nothing contradicts it.

cases.vignette: 60-year-old man born in December 1965, seen by his family physician at his primary care practice for an annual wellness visit.
