cases.vignette: 62-year-old man who received a heart transplant 4 months ago at a hospital that is not Medicare-approved for heart transplantation, so the transplant was not covered. He has since been discharged and now requests coverage for routine post-transplant follow-up: clinic visits with his transplant cardiologist, laboratory monitoring, and echocardiography, which his physicians document as reasonable and necessary.
cases.note: Follow-up care is covered even though the transplant itself was noncovered.

cases.vignette: 64-year-old woman with end-stage non-ischemic cardiomyopathy who meets her center's transplant listing criteria. The hospital performing the transplant has run a heart transplant program for 6 years with good outcomes but has not been approved by Medicare as meeting the institutional coverage criteria for heart transplant facilities.
cases.note: Facility is not Medicare-approved for heart transplantation.

cases.vignette: 58-year-old man with end-stage heart failure scheduled for heart transplant at a hospital whose heart transplant program began 18 months ago. The hospital is not Medicare-approved and has asked CMS for an exception to the facility criteria, citing strong early outcomes.
cases.note: Program only 18 months old and not approved; exceptions are barred for programs under 2 years.

cases.vignette: 61-year-old woman listed for heart transplant. The transplant will be performed at one of three independent community hospitals that pooled their cases into a heart transplant consortium. The hospitals are not under common control or a formal affiliation, do not share the same transplant team, and applied to Medicare for approval as a consortium.
cases.note: Consortium arrangement of independent hospitals; consortia are not approved.

cases.vignette: 14-year-old Medicare beneficiary (entitled through end-stage renal disease) with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and end-stage heart failure, scheduled for heart transplant at a pediatric hospital that performs pediatric heart transplants. The pediatric hospital operates its program independently, without a joint program with any Medicare-approved heart transplant facility, and has not submitted an application to CMS.
cases.note: Pediatric hospital operates alone and has no CMS-approved application.

cases.vignette: 66-year-old man with end-stage ischemic cardiomyopathy who has been matched with a donor heart. The request identifies the hospital performing the transplant and includes the patient's clinical evaluation, but contains no information on whether the hospital's heart transplant program is approved by Medicare.
cases.note: Transplant hospital named, but its Medicare approval status is not documented.

cases.vignette: 16-year-old Medicare beneficiary (entitled through end-stage renal disease) with restrictive cardiomyopathy awaiting heart transplant at a pediatric hospital that performs pediatric heart transplants. The hospital states that its program is run jointly with a Medicare-approved adult heart transplant center and shares its surgeons, but the request contains no documentation of whether the hospital submitted an application to CMS or whether CMS approved it.
cases.note: Pediatric hospital; joint program described, but no record of a CMS-approved application.

cases.vignette: 82-year-old woman with severe bilateral hip osteoarthritis. Without support she cannot walk safely to the bathroom or kitchen; she fell twice in the past month while trying to reach the toilet. Cognition and vision are intact. In a physical therapy evaluation, a properly fitted standard walker let her walk safely throughout her single-level home and complete toileting, dressing, grooming, and meal preparation in a reasonable time. She is willing and able to use it consistently. Her physician documents these findings and orders a standard walker.
cases.note: Walker resolves an in-home mobility deficit safely; cognition intact.

cases.vignette: 70-year-old man with a right above-knee amputation who cannot use a prosthesis because of a non-healing residual-limb wound. He cannot reach the bathroom or kitchen in his home without help. In a fitted walker trial he could hop only 3 meters before resting and lost balance twice; a cane is unsafe. Cognition and vision are intact. He has full upper-extremity strength and range of motion and, in a fitted lightweight manual wheelchair, propelled himself throughout his single-level home, which has wide doorways and hard floors, completing toileting, dressing, and meals safely. His physician documents this and orders a manual wheelchair.
cases.note: Manual wheelchair: cane/walker trial unsafe, strong upper extremities, accessible home, safe operation shown.

cases.vignette: 75-year-old man with lumbar spinal stenosis who walks safely throughout his home with a rollator walker and independently completes toileting, bathing, dressing, grooming, and feeding in a reasonable time. Cognition and vision are intact. He becomes fatigued after walking about 150 meters outdoors and wants to be able to go to the grocery store and shopping mall. His physician orders a power wheelchair for community mobility.
cases.note: Walker resolves all in-home MRADLs; the power wheelchair is wanted for community trips, which the NCD does not consider.

cases.vignette: 73-year-old woman with advanced multiple sclerosis who cannot walk, even with a walker, and cannot self-propel a manual wheelchair because of severe upper-extremity weakness and fatigue. She lacks the trunk control to sit safely on a scooter. Cognition and vision are intact and she safely operated a power wheelchair with a joystick in the clinic. She lives alone. A therapist's home evaluation found that her apartment's bathroom and bedroom doorways are too narrow for the power wheelchair, there are steps between rooms, and the chair could be used only in the entry hall; no modifications are planned. Her physician orders a power wheelchair.
cases.note: Home environment cannot support the power wheelchair (confirmed by home evaluation).

cases.vignette: 86-year-old man with severe heart failure and knee arthritis who cannot walk more than a few steps even with a walker, and lacks the arm strength to propel a manual wheelchair. He is legally blind from end-stage macular degeneration and in a clinic trial repeatedly struck walls, furniture, and a staff member with a power wheelchair because he could not see obstacles. Low-vision rehabilitation has been tried without improvement. He lives alone; no family member or other caregiver is available. His physician orders a power wheelchair.
cases.note: Severe visual impairment prevents effective use, with no caregiver or other compensation. The failed clinic trial also shows he cannot operate it safely.

cases.vignette: 63-year-old woman on Medicare through disability with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. She has no functional use of her legs and cannot stand, so her physician documents that a cane or walker is clearly precluded and no trial was done. Grip strength is 2/5 and she cannot propel a manual wheelchair more than 1 meter. She cannot sit upright without trunk support and so cannot safely operate a scooter. She needs a power wheelchair with joystick control and a tilt-in-space seat to reach the bathroom, kitchen, and bedroom. Cognition is intact. She lives with her husband, who cannot push a manual wheelchair because of his own spinal condition. A home evaluation confirmed doorways, turning space, and floor surfaces accommodate the power wheelchair, and she drove it safely during a home trial. Her physician documents all of this and orders the power wheelchair.
cases.note: Power wheelchair: non-ambulatory (no cane/walker trial needed), cannot self-propel, no POV trunk stability, needs joystick features, accessible home, safe.

cases.vignette: 84-year-old woman with advanced Parkinson's disease who cannot walk safely even with a fitted walker (three falls in the trial) and cannot reach her bathroom or kitchen without help. Her arm strength and coordination are too poor to propel a manual wheelchair herself. Her husband, who lives with her and is home all day, is willing and able to push the wheelchair, transfer her safely to and from it, and has demonstrated this in therapy. Their single-level home has wide doorways and hard floors. Cognition is adequate to participate. Her physician documents this and orders a manual wheelchair to be operated by her husband.
cases.note: Cannot self-propel, but a consistently available, willing, able caregiver makes a manual wheelchair appropriate.

cases.vignette: 71-year-old man with severe COPD who cannot walk more than 10 meters even with a walker because of dyspnea and cannot self-propel a manual wheelchair for the same reason. Cognition and vision are intact. He has good trunk stability, strong arms, and in a home trial operated a scooter (POV) safely through every room needed for toileting, bathing, dressing, and meals; his home accommodates the scooter. He needs no joystick, special seating, or low seat height. He prefers a power wheelchair because it is smaller, and his physician orders a power wheelchair.
cases.note: Patient can safely operate a POV in the home; power wheelchair features are not needed.

cases.vignette: 78-year-old woman with a right hemiparesis from stroke and severe left shoulder arthritis who cannot walk safely with a cane or hemi-walker. In a fitted manual wheelchair, including a one-arm-drive model, she could not propel herself more than a meter. She lives alone and has no family member or other caregiver available to push the chair. Her single-level home is wheelchair accessible. Her physician orders a standard manual wheelchair.
cases.note: Manual wheelchair requested but the patient cannot self-propel and has no caregiver to push it.

cases.vignette: 66-year-old man on Medicare through disability with a C6 incomplete spinal cord injury. He cannot walk and cannot use a cane or walker, cannot propel a manual wheelchair because of weak hands and arms, and lacks the trunk stability for a scooter. He needs a power wheelchair with joystick control to reach his bathroom and kitchen. Cognition and vision are intact, and he drove a power wheelchair safely during a clinic assessment. He lives with his wife. The physician's documentation and the therapy evaluation describe only the clinic assessment; there is no information about his home's layout, doorways, surfaces, or whether a power wheelchair can be used there.
cases.note: Clinical need for a power wheelchair documented, but nothing in the record addresses the home environment.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old woman with spinal muscular atrophy who cannot walk with any device, cannot self-propel a manual wheelchair, and lacks the trunk control for a scooter; she needs a power wheelchair with joystick control to reach her bathroom, bedroom, and kitchen. Cognition and vision are intact. A home evaluation found her single-level home accessible for a power wheelchair. She lives with her daughter, who works full time. No trial or assessment of her operating a power wheelchair, in the clinic or at home, is documented. Her physician orders a power wheelchair.
cases.note: No assessment of the patient's ability to operate the power wheelchair safely is documented.

cases.vignette: 67-year-old woman with secondary lymphedema of the left arm (ICD-10-CM I97.2) after mastectomy and axillary node dissection 3 years ago. She completed exactly 4 weeks of conservative therapy: daily wear of a graduated compression sleeve, a prescribed arm exercise program, and elevation of the limb. Her physician documents that significant swelling and heaviness remain, with arm circumference 5 cm greater than the right side at three measured points. The physician's determination records her diagnosis and prognosis, these measurements, the failed trial, and her response to an initial in-office session with a nonsegmented pneumatic compression pump: circumference reduced 1.5 cm, the session was well tolerated at the planned pressure, and she applied the sleeve herself. The physician prescribes the device with a written plan for pressure, frequency, and duration, arranges instruction, and will monitor use and response.
cases.note: Boundary: exactly four-week lymphedema trial with all three components; all physician documentation present.

cases.vignette: 73-year-old man with chronic venous insufficiency of the right leg and a venous stasis ulcer above the medial malleolus (ICD-10-CM I87.311) present for 9 months. For the past 7 months his physician has directed conservative therapy: multilayer compression bandaging, moist wound dressings appropriate to the ulcer, a calf-muscle exercise program, and leg elevation. The ulcer remains open, measuring 3.2 x 2.5 cm. The physician's determination records his diagnosis and prognosis, the ulcer and limb measurements, the failed treatments, and his response to an initial treatment with a nonsegmented pneumatic compression device (tolerated, edema reduced, his wife can apply it). The physician prescribes the device with a treatment plan defining pressure, frequency, and duration and will monitor his use and response.
cases.note: CVI with a venous ulcer unhealed after 7 months of complete physician-directed conservative therapy.

cases.vignette: 70-year-old woman with chronic venous insufficiency of both legs, with hyperpigmentation, stasis dermatitis, and chronic ankle edema, but no ulcers now or in the past. Over 8 months her physician directed compression stockings, exercise, and leg elevation with only partial relief. The physician's determination records her diagnosis, prognosis, ankle circumference measurements, failed treatments, and a good response to an initial treatment with a pneumatic compression device. The physician prescribes the device for home use with a treatment plan and ongoing monitoring.
cases.note: CVI signs (pigmentation, edema, dermatitis) but no venous stasis ulcer.

cases.vignette: 76-year-old man with chronic venous insufficiency and a venous stasis ulcer of the left lower leg. Four months ago his physician started conservative therapy with compression bandaging, wound dressings, exercise, and leg elevation; the ulcer is smaller but not healed. He has no lymphedema. The physician's determination records diagnosis, prognosis, ulcer measurements, treatments tried, and his response to an initial treatment with a pneumatic compression device. The physician prescribes the device for home use with a treatment plan and monitoring.
cases.note: Venous ulcer, but conservative trial only 4 months; the 4-week lymphedema rule does not apply to CVI.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old woman with primary lymphedema of both legs. Over 6 weeks she followed an exercise program and elevated her legs several times a day, but she declined compression garments and bandages because she finds them uncomfortable, so none were used. Significant swelling remains. The physician's determination records diagnosis, prognosis, calf and thigh circumference measurements, treatments tried, and her response to an initial treatment with a nonsegmented pneumatic compression device. The physician prescribes the device with a treatment plan and monitoring.
cases.note: Lymphedema trial lasted 6 weeks but omitted compression (patient declined garments and bandages).

cases.vignette: 72-year-old woman with secondary lymphedema of the right leg after pelvic lymph node dissection. She completed a 6-week trial of a compression garment, exercise, and elevation, with significant swelling remaining. The physician's determination records diagnosis, prognosis, limb measurements, the failed trial, and a good response to an initial treatment with a nonsegmented pump and segmented appliance. Her physician nonetheless orders a segmented, calibrated gradient pneumatic compression device (HCPCS E0652) because he considers it the most advanced model; the record identifies no characteristic of the patient that would prevent satisfactory treatment with a nonsegmented device with a segmented appliance or a segmented device without manual pressure control.
cases.note: E0652 requested without any unique characteristics; a simpler device was never shown unsatisfactory.

cases.vignette: 64-year-old man on Medicare through disability with secondary lymphedema of the left leg after groin dissection and radiation. A 4-week trial of compression bandaging, exercise, and elevation left significant swelling. His leg has a dense radiation-fibrosis band at the upper thigh with fragile skin grafts below it. His physician documents trials of a nonsegmented device with a segmented appliance and of a segmented device without manual pressure control: both pushed fluid against the fibrotic band, causing genital edema and graft breakdown, and treatment had to stop. The physician concludes these characteristics require individually set pressures per chamber and orders a segmented, calibrated gradient device (HCPCS E0652). His response to an initial session with it (reduced circumference, no genital edema, tolerated) is recorded with his diagnosis, prognosis, and measurements. There is a written treatment plan, instruction, and ongoing monitoring.
cases.note: E0652 exception: documented unique characteristics prevented satisfactory treatment with both simpler device types.

cases.vignette: 71-year-old woman with secondary lymphedema of the right arm after breast cancer treatment. She completed 5 weeks of a compression sleeve, exercise, and elevation; her physician documents that significant swelling remains, with circumference 4 cm greater than the left arm at the forearm and upper arm. The physician's determination records her diagnosis and prognosis, the measurements, and the failed trial, and the physician prescribes a nonsegmented pneumatic compression device with a treatment plan, instruction, and monitoring. The record contains no initial treatment session with the device or any description of her response to one.
cases.note: All criteria met except that no response to an initial treatment with the device is documented.

cases.vignette: 74-year-old man with secondary lymphedema of the left leg after prostate cancer surgery and radiation. He completed a 6-week trial of a compression garment, exercise, and leg elevation, and his physician documents that significant swelling and heaviness remain. The physician's note records his diagnosis and prognosis, the failed trial, and that an initial treatment with a nonsegmented pump was tolerated, reduced swelling, and can be applied by his wife. The physician prescribes the device with a treatment plan and monitoring. The physical examination describes the leg only as 'swollen'; no circumference, volume, or other measurements are recorded anywhere.
cases.note: No objective measurements of severity documented; narrative only.

cases.vignette: 68-year-old woman discharged home 2 days after a total knee replacement. Her surgeon prescribes a pneumatic compression device for both legs for 3 weeks at home to prevent deep vein thrombosis. She has no lymphedema, no chronic venous insufficiency, and no leg ulcers. The surgeon documents the indication and gives instructions for use.
cases.note: DVT prophylaxis after knee replacement is neither lymphedema nor CVI with ulcer.

cases.vignette: 77-year-old man with severe COPD (ICD-10-CM J44.9, FEV1 28% predicted) and orthopnea. He becomes acutely short of breath within minutes of lying flat and must sleep every night with his head and trunk elevated at least 30-45 degrees; pillows and a foam wedge in his ordinary bed slide out of position and have not worked. The physician's prescription, submitted with the initial claim, names the COPD, describes nightly orthopnea with desaturation to 85% when flat, and orders a manual (crank-adjusted) hospital bed for positioning.
cases.note: COPD requiring nightly head elevation not achievable with pillows; prescription states condition, severity, frequency.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old woman recovering at home from a cervical spine injury who requires continuous cervical traction in bed for 6 weeks. The traction apparatus mounts on a bed frame and the supplier documents that it cannot be fixed to or used on her ordinary bed. The physician's prescription, submitted with the initial claim, describes the cervical injury and specifies the traction frame attachment that requires a hospital bed, and orders a manual hospital bed.
cases.note: Special attachment that cannot be used on an ordinary bed; prescription names the condition and the attachment.

cases.vignette: 84-year-old woman with mild knee osteoarthritis who sleeps comfortably flat in her ordinary bed and needs no special positioning or attachments. Her daughter requests a hospital bed because it would make it easier for her mother to get in and out of bed and easier for the daughter to change the sheets. The physician's prescription, submitted with the claim, states 'osteoarthritis of knees, hospital bed for convenience of transfers and care.'
cases.note: No positioning need or attachment; requested for ease of getting in and out of bed and caregiver convenience.

cases.vignette: 81-year-old man with congestive heart failure. The physician's prescription, submitted with the initial claim, reads 'Hospital bed. Diagnosis: CHF. Patient requires positioning.' No other documentation is submitted; the record does not describe his symptoms, how severe they are, or how often they occur.
cases.note: Positioning need stated with a diagnosis, but no severity or frequency of symptoms anywhere in the documentation.

cases.vignette: 79-year-old woman with severe rheumatoid arthritis who already has a covered manual hospital bed for positioning to relieve joint pain. She now needs frequent position changes through the night. She has fixed ulnar deviation and flexion contractures of all fingers and cannot press or hold any bed control; her husband would operate the controls for her. She has no spinal cord injury and no brain injury or other neurologic disease. The supplier requests coverage of electric powered head and foot adjustments.
cases.note: Patient cannot operate the controls and has neither spinal cord injury nor brain damage, so the exception does not apply.

cases.vignette: 72-year-old man with severe heart failure (LVEF 20%) who already has a covered hospital bed for positioning. He has episodes of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea 3-4 nights per week in which he wakes gasping and must be upright immediately; turning the manual crank or waiting for help takes several minutes and has led to two emergency calls. He has normal hand function and can operate a bed control pendant himself. The physician documents the condition, the frequency and severity of the episodes, and that no delay in repositioning can be tolerated. The supplier requests coverage of electric powered head and foot adjustments.
cases.note: Electric adjustments: immediate need for position change (no delay tolerated) and the patient can operate the controls.

cases.vignette: 74-year-old woman with COPD who has a covered manual hospital bed for nightly head elevation. Her positioning need is unchanged all night: the head of the bed is raised once at bedtime and lowered once in the morning, and she has no episodes requiring urgent repositioning. She can operate controls. She would prefer electric controls because the hand crank is tiring for her husband. The supplier requests coverage of electric powered head and foot adjustments.
cases.note: Positioning is needed once nightly with no frequent or immediate need; electric adjustment is a convenience.

cases.vignette: 88-year-old man with end-stage dementia who is completely bedbound, does not sit on the edge of the bed, does not stand, ambulate, or transfer to a chair or wheelchair, and has no cardiac disease. He has a covered manual hospital bed for positioning to prevent contractures. His caregiver requests a variable height feature so the bed can be raised to make bathing him easier on her back.
cases.note: Bedbound patient who neither ambulates nor transfers; variable height matches none of the listed conditions.

cases.vignette: 67-year-old man with C6 quadriplegia who must be repositioned every 2 hours, around the clock, with his body aligned in ways an ordinary bed cannot provide, to prevent contractures and pressure injuries. Home-health nursing notes describing his condition and repositioning schedule are attached to the supplier's initial claim for a manual hospital bed. No physician's prescription is included with the claim or anywhere in the submitted records.
cases.note: Clinical need appears met, but no physician's prescription accompanies the initial claim.

cases.vignette: 58-year-old woman on Medicare through disability with C5 quadriplegia from a diving injury. She must be repositioned every 2 hours day and night with specific trunk and limb alignment and periodic head elevation to prevent contractures, pressure injuries, and aspiration pneumonia; this cannot be done in her ordinary bed. She cannot use her hands, and her caregivers do all repositioning. The physician's prescription, submitted with the initial claim, describes the quadriplegia, the repositioning frequency, and the severity of her contracture and aspiration risk, and orders a manual hospital bed.
cases.note: Quadriplegia with positioning every 2 hours; documented. The patient's inability to operate controls is irrelevant for a manual bed.

cases.vignette: 79-year-old woman, bedridden after a large left hemispheric stroke, with a stage 4 sacral pressure ulcer (ICD-10-CM L89.154). For the past 6 weeks at home she has received a full conservative program: repositioning every 2 hours, a Group II powered pressure-reducing mattress, antibiotic treatment of a wound infection that has resolved, nutrition optimization with a dietitian, sharp debridement, and moist dressings under an occlusive film. The ulcer has not progressed toward healing. Her attending physician completed a comprehensive assessment, documented that she would need nursing-home placement without an air-fluidized bed, considered and ruled out other support surfaces, and gave the supplier a written order before delivery. Her daughter, a trained adult caregiver, lives with her and will provide all required care. The home has a concrete slab floor and electrical capacity confirmed adequate. She has no lung disease. The physician will direct the home regimen and recertify the need monthly.
cases.note: All criteria met after 6 weeks of complete conservative treatment.

cases.vignette: 83-year-old man with advanced Parkinson's disease who is bedridden, with a stage 4 ischial pressure ulcer. His conservative treatment ran for 5 weeks: the first 2 weeks in a skilled nursing facility (whose records document repositioning every 2 hours, a Group II support surface, treatment of wound infection, nutrition optimization, and debridement) and the next 3 weeks at home with the same program. The ulcer has not progressed toward healing. Wet-to-dry dressings for debridement started in the SNF and are still being used 35 days later; other dressings are moist and covered with an occlusive film. His attending physician completed a comprehensive evaluation, documented that he would require readmission to a nursing facility without an air-fluidized bed, ruled out all other equipment, and sent the supplier a written order before delivery. His wife, a trained caregiver, provides all care at home. The home's floor structure and wiring are adequate. He has no pulmonary disease. The physician directs the home regimen and recertifies monthly.
cases.note: Two exceptions: part of the conservative month was in a SNF (documented), and wet-to-dry debridement continues past 30 days.

cases.vignette: 71-year-old man on Medicare through disability with T4 paraplegia who is chair bound, with a stage 3 pressure ulcer over the right greater trochanter. A complete conservative program was started exactly one month before the order: repositioning every 2 hours, a Group II air mattress, treatment of a resolved cellulitis, nutrition optimization, enzymatic debridement, and moist dressings under occlusive covering. At the end of that month the wound showed no progression toward healing. His attending physician completed a comprehensive assessment, documented that he would otherwise require institutional care, ruled out alternative equipment, and furnished the written order to the supplier before delivery. His adult son, trained in all required care, lives with him. Structural and electrical capacity of the home are adequate, and he has no pulmonary disease. The physician will recertify monthly.
cases.note: Boundary: conservative treatment exactly one month; stage 3 ulcer.

cases.vignette: 80-year-old woman, bedridden from end-stage dementia, with a stage 4 sacral pressure ulcer. A conservative program was started 3 weeks ago: repositioning every 2 hours, a Group II support surface, infection treatment, nutrition optimization, debridement, and occlusive moist dressings. Because the wound is large, her physician wrote an order for an air-fluidized bed now. He documented a comprehensive evaluation, that she would otherwise need nursing-home placement, and that alternative equipment was ruled out; the written order reached the supplier before delivery. Her husband is a trained caregiver. Home structure and electrical capacity are adequate. She has no lung disease. Monthly physician recertification is planned.
cases.note: Conservative treatment lasted only 3 weeks before the order.

cases.vignette: 76-year-old man, bedridden after a spinal cord infarction, with a stage 4 sacral pressure ulcer. Six weeks of complete conservative treatment (repositioning every 2 hours, a Group II mattress, infection treatment, nutrition optimization, debridement, occlusive moist dressings) produced no progression toward healing. His attending physician documented a comprehensive assessment, that he would need institutional care without the bed, and that other equipment was ruled out, and furnished the written order to the supplier before delivery. His wife is a trained caregiver. The home is structurally and electrically adequate. His problem list includes moderate COPD for which he uses a long-acting bronchodilator inhaler daily. Monthly recertification is planned.
cases.note: Coexisting COPD (pulmonary disease) is an explicit home-use exclusion, hidden among satisfied criteria.

cases.vignette: 84-year-old woman, bedridden after a hip fracture with failed repair, with a stage 4 sacral pressure ulcer. Seven weeks of complete conservative treatment (repositioning every 2 hours, a Group II support surface, infection treatment, nutrition optimization, debridement, occlusive moist dressings) produced no progression toward healing. Her attending physician completed a comprehensive evaluation, documented that she would otherwise need nursing-home placement, and ruled out alternatives. Her niece is a trained caregiver living with her; the home is structurally and electrically adequate; she has no pulmonary disease; monthly recertification is planned. The supplier delivered the air-fluidized bed on the physician's telephone order; the signed written order was faxed to the supplier 3 days after delivery.
cases.note: Bed delivered on a verbal order; the written order reached the supplier after delivery.

cases.vignette: 78-year-old man, bedridden from advanced multiple sclerosis, with a stage 4 sacral pressure ulcer. Six weeks of conservative treatment (repositioning every 2 hours, a Group II mattress, infection treatment, nutrition optimization, debridement) produced no progression toward healing. His wound care plan requires continuous wet saline-soaked gauze packing changed three times daily, left open to air without any plastic wrap or occlusive covering because of periwound skin breakdown. The attending physician documented a comprehensive evaluation, that he would otherwise require institutional care, and that alternatives were ruled out, and sent a written order to the supplier before delivery. His wife is a trained caregiver; the home is structurally and electrically adequate; he has no pulmonary disease; monthly recertification is planned.
cases.note: Wound care requires wet saline soaks without an occlusive covering (not the wet-to-dry exception).

cases.vignette: 81-year-old woman, bedridden after multiple strokes, with a stage 3 sacral pressure ulcer. For 6 weeks she has been repositioned every 2 hours on her standard home foam mattress, with infection treatment, nutrition optimization, debridement, and occlusive moist dressings. No pressure-reducing support surface of any kind was used. The ulcer has not progressed toward healing. Her attending physician completed a comprehensive assessment, documented that she would otherwise need nursing-home placement, and furnished a written order for an air-fluidized bed to the supplier before delivery. Her son is a trained caregiver; the home is structurally and electrically adequate; she has no pulmonary disease; monthly recertification is planned.
cases.note: Conservative treatment used only a standard foam mattress; no Group II support surface.

cases.vignette: 77-year-old man, bedridden from ALS, with a stage 4 sacral pressure ulcer. Six weeks of complete conservative treatment (repositioning every 2 hours, a Group II mattress, infection treatment, nutrition optimization, debridement, occlusive moist dressings) produced no progression toward healing. His attending physician completed a comprehensive evaluation, documented that he would otherwise need institutional care, ruled out alternative equipment, and furnished the written order to the supplier before delivery. The home is structurally and electrically adequate, he has no pulmonary disease, and monthly recertification is planned. The caregiver section of the home assessment form is blank, and no note identifies anyone who will provide or be trained to provide his care at home.
cases.note: The record does not address who will care for the patient at home; nothing says no caregiver exists.

cases.vignette: 74-year-old woman, chair bound and bedridden after a high spinal cord injury, with a stage 4 coccygeal pressure ulcer. The physician's notes describe 5 weeks of conservative treatment with repositioning every 2 hours, treatment of a wound infection, nutrition optimization with protein supplementation, sharp debridement, and moist dressings under an occlusive covering, with no progression toward healing. The notes do not state what mattress or support surface she used during that period. The attending physician documented a comprehensive evaluation, that she would otherwise need nursing-home care, that other equipment was considered and ruled out, and furnished a written order for an air-fluidized bed to the supplier before delivery. Her husband is a trained caregiver; home structure and electrical capacity are adequate; she has no pulmonary disease; monthly recertification is planned.
cases.note: Conservative-treatment notes list every component except the support surface, which is not mentioned either way.

cases.vignette: 68-year-old man with type 1 diabetes, ICD-10-CM E10.65. Fasting C-peptide is undetectable (below the lab's lower limit of normal) with a concurrent fasting glucose of 162 mg/dL. He completed a comprehensive diabetes education program 3 years ago and has used multiple daily injections (basal plus three prandial injections daily) with frequent self-adjustment of doses for 4 years. His meter download shows an average of 5.2 glucose checks per day over the last 2 months. His HbA1c on this regimen is 8.1%. The pump is ordered by an endocrinologist who manages over 100 CSII patients with a team of diabetes nurses, educators, and a dietitian. Request: external insulin pump (CSII) and supplies for home use.
cases.note: Criterion A fully met; C-peptide undetectable with valid glucose; HbA1c 8.1%.

cases.vignette: 74-year-old woman with long-standing insulin-treated type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease with a measured creatinine clearance of 45 mL/min. Fasting C-peptide is 180% of the laboratory's lower limit of normal, drawn with a concurrent fasting glucose of 190 mg/dL; GAD65 antibodies are negative. She completed a comprehensive diabetes education program and has been on four insulin injections daily with frequent self-adjustment for 2 years. Meter logs show an average of 4.6 checks per day over the last 2 months. On this regimen she has had recurring hypoglycemia (three to four episodes below 54 mg/dL per month). An endocrinologist experienced with many CSII patients, working with a CSII nurse, educator, and dietitian, orders an external insulin pump for home use.
cases.note: C-peptide 180% of LLN fails the usual 110% cutoff but meets the 200% cutoff because creatinine clearance is 45 mL/min; recurring hypoglycemia satisfies Criterion A.

cases.vignette: 70-year-old man with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes and a creatinine clearance of 82 mL/min. Fasting C-peptide is 150% of the laboratory's lower limit of normal with a concurrent fasting glucose of 150 mg/dL; GAD65, IA-2, and ZnT8 antibodies are all negative. He completed comprehensive diabetes education, has used three to four insulin injections daily with frequent self-adjustment for 18 months, and his meter shows an average of 4.8 checks per day over the past 2 months. HbA1c is 8.6%. An endocrinologist experienced with many CSII patients and supported by a CSII team orders an external insulin pump.
cases.note: Normal renal function, so the 110% cutoff applies; C-peptide 150% of LLN and antibodies negative.

cases.vignette: 67-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes; fasting C-peptide is undetectable with a concurrent fasting glucose of 140 mg/dL. She completed a comprehensive diabetes education program and has used multiple daily injections (four per day) with frequent self-adjustment for 6 years. Her HbA1c is 7.9% and she reports wide fluctuations in pre-meal glucose. Her meter download for the past 2 months shows an average of 3.1 glucose checks per day. An endocrinologist who manages many CSII patients with a team of nurses, educators, and dietitians orders an external insulin pump.
cases.note: Self-testing averages 3.1/day over the prior 2 months; at least 4/day is required.

cases.vignette: 65-year-old man with type 1 diabetes who has used an insulin pump for 9 years through his employer plan and just enrolled in Medicare. His meter records for the month before Medicare enrollment show an average of 4.3 glucose checks per day. GAD65 antibodies are positive; no C-peptide test is on file. His endocrinologist, who manages over 80 pump patients with a team of diabetes nurses, educators, and a dietitian, orders an external insulin pump and supplies for home use under Medicare.
cases.note: Criterion B: on a pump before Medicare enrollment with >= 4 checks/day the month before; antibody positive substitutes for C-peptide.

cases.vignette: 71-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes; fasting C-peptide is below the lab's lower limit of normal with concurrent fasting glucose of 132 mg/dL. She completed a comprehensive diabetes education program and has used four daily insulin injections with frequent self-adjustment for 3 years; meter data show 5.5 checks per day over the past 2 months. Her HbA1c on this regimen is 7.0%. Her physician documents no history of recurring hypoglycemia, stable pre-meal glucose values, no dawn phenomenon (fasting values 100-140 mg/dL), and no severe glycemic excursions. She wants a pump for convenience. An endocrinologist experienced with many CSII patients and a CSII team orders an external insulin pump.
cases.note: Boundary: HbA1c exactly 7.0% is not > 7.0%, and none of the other qualifying glycemic criteria are present.

cases.vignette: 59-year-old woman on Medicare through disability with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis and chronic intractable lower-extremity spasticity. Over the past 8 weeks she tried oral baclofen at maximum dose plus tizanidine; spasticity remained uncontrolled (Modified Ashworth 4 in both legs) and she had intolerable sedation. A trial intrathecal bolus of baclofen reduced her Ashworth scores to 1-2 for 8 hours. She has no allergy to baclofen, no active infection, adequate body size for the device, and no other implanted programmable devices. Her neurologist requests implantation of a programmable infusion pump for intrathecal baclofen.
cases.note: Intrathecal baclofen pump: 8-week oral trial failed, favorable intrathecal test dose, no contraindications.

cases.vignette: 63-year-old man on Medicare through disability with spastic paraparesis after a thoracic spinal cord injury. A 10-week trial of oral baclofen and dantrolene failed to control spasticity. A trial intrathecal dose of baclofen produced marked improvement. He has no drug allergy, no active infection, and adequate body size. He has had a programmable implanted spinal cord stimulator for neuropathic pain for 4 years, which will remain in place. His physiatrist requests implantation of an intrathecal baclofen infusion pump.
cases.note: Implanted programmable spinal cord stimulator: implantation is contraindicated with other implanted programmable devices.

cases.vignette: 69-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer and severe intractable abdominal and back pain despite high-dose oral and transdermal opioids with intolerable sedation. A temporary intrathecal catheter trial of morphine gave good pain relief with acceptable side effects, and he accepts the therapy. His oncologist documents an estimated life expectancy of about 6 weeks. He has no active infection, drug allergy, or other implanted devices. His pain physician requests implantation of an intrathecal opioid infusion pump.
cases.note: Life expectancy about 6 weeks, below the required 3 months, despite a successful trial.

cases.vignette: 66-year-old woman with severe chronic intractable low back and leg pain of nonmalignant origin after three spinal surgeries. Her history documents inadequate relief and intolerable side effects from systemic opioids and adjuvant medications, plus completed behavioral pain management. She has no life-limiting illness, no active infection, no drug allergy, adequate body size, and no other implanted devices. Her pain physician requests implantation of an intrathecal morphine infusion pump. The record contains the history, medication list, and psychology note, and no documentation of any intraspinal opioid trial.
cases.note: No record of a preliminary trial with a temporary intraspinal catheter; nothing contradicts it.

cases.vignette: 72-year-old man with type 1 diabetes; fasting C-peptide is undetectable with a concurrent fasting glucose of 170 mg/dL. He completed a comprehensive diabetes education program and has used four daily insulin injections with frequent self-adjustment for 5 years. His HbA1c is 8.4%. An endocrinologist who manages many CSII patients with a team of CSII-knowledgeable nurses, educators, and dietitians orders an external insulin pump. The submitted records include the lab results and clinic notes; there are no meter downloads, logs, or notes about how often he checks his glucose.
cases.note: Glucose self-testing frequency is not documented anywhere; other Criterion A elements are met.
